newsitem.title: UK: IRA truce hopes fade as Major rejects peace plan.
newsitem.headline: IRA truce hopes fade as Major rejects peace plan.

text.p: Hopes for a new Irish Republican Army (IRA) ceasefire faded on Tuesday after British Prime Minister John Major effectively rejected peace proposals by Northern Irish Catholic leaders.

Major's office said he had written to John Hume, leader of the moderate nationalist Social Democratic and Labour Party, saying the government was not prepared to relax its conditions for the IRA's political arm, Sinn Fein, to join talks on the future of Northern Ireland.
Hume together with Sinn Fein had set out proposals they said would persuade the IRA to end its guerrilla campaign for a united Ireland if accepted.

"It is not a question of acceptance or rejection... We have reasserted the existing policy of the British government. There has never been any question of negotiating a new position," Major's office said in a statement.
Sinn Fein leader Gerry Adams said Major's apparent rejection of the proposals meant the IRA would not resume a 17-month truce it abandoned in February.
"I don't think there is any evidence the IRA is proposing any unilateral initiatives," Adams told reporters.
Sinn Fein's chairman Mitchel McLaughlin has already warned Major he would be making a "lethal miscalculation" if he rejected the plan.
Under the proposals, Sinn Fein would have been allowed into the talks as soon as the IRA called an "unequivocal" ceasefire.
Sinn Fein and the SDLP also wanted Britain to drop demands that the guerrillas disarm before the negotiations and called on Major to set a fixed timetable for the talks.
They also wanted goodwill gestures from Britain, such as the release of IRA prisoners.

Hume told the BBC in Brussels he believed the proposals had been scuppered by Major's reliance on Northern Irish Protestant politicians to bolster his support in parliament. Major has a parliamentary majority of just one.

"The numbers game in Westminster (parliament) because of an absence of a real majority by the government and the imminence of a general election have all been factors that have made my job in achieving a real cessation (of violence by the IRA) more difficult," said Hume.
"That rather disturbs me because I would rather have hoped that everyone would have put peace first."

Pro-British "Loyalists" who have been allowed to take part in the talks because their own guerrillas are still honouring a two-year ceasefire, are fiercely opposed to any relaxation of the conditions for Sinn Fein's entry into the negotiations.

They have warned they will walk out of the talks, while unionist politicians in the British parliament have threatened to withdraw their support from Major if he grants any concessions to Sinn Fein or the IRA.

Under pressure from the unionists, Major last year rejected a proposal by the chairman of the talks, former U.S. senator George Mitchell, that "decommissioning" of guerrilla arms be addressed during the talks.
London's insistence that disarmament should come first provoked the IRA into ending its truce and launching a series of bombings on British targets, which have claimed four lives since February.
